column1: # Escalation edges. Tab separated. Adding one should be a data change, not a code change.
# trigger        the role name, application permission, or data-plane capability
# needs          resource type that must also be visible, or blank for none
# reaches        what taking the edge would get you
# precondition   what has to be true beyond the trigger, in plain words
# Every row is an inference. Nothing here is taken -- the tool reports the edge
# and stops. Taking it is a decision for a human with a scope document.

column5: any role at that scope, including roles the credential does not currently hold
column6: Owner carries Microsoft.Authorization/roleAssignments/write, so the ceiling is the scope, not the role
User Access Administrator is roleAssignments/write with no data access of its own, which makes it easy to under-rate

column5: the VM managed identity and every role assigned to it
column6: the VM must have an identity assigned; runCommand executes as SYSTEM or root without touching the guest credentials

column5: the Automation Account managed identity, and any credential stored in the account
column6: runbook creation and execution is a Contributor operation

column5: the App Service or Function managed identity, plus deployment credentials
column6: publishxml returns a publish profile containing usable credentials

column5: the Logic App managed identity and every API connection it holds
column6: API connections often carry consented access to third-party SaaS

column5: cluster admin credentials and the kubelet identity
column6: listClusterAdminCredential is available to Contributor unless local accounts are disabled
a new container group can be created with an existing user-assigned identity attached

column5: account keys via listKeys, and every SAS derivable from them
column6: an account key outlives the role assignment; it stays valid until someone rotates it

column5: data-plane access to vault contents by adding the principal to the access policy
column6: only on vaults still using the access policy model; RBAC vaults do not honour policy edits

column5: image pull and push, which is the build supply chain for anything consuming the registry
column6: pushing a tag consumers already pull is the quiet version of this

column5: tenant-wide compromise: add a credential to any service principal and authenticate as it
column6: this is the single highest-value application permission in Entra and it is routinely granted to automation

column5: any application permission, self-granted, including Directory.ReadWrite.All
column6: the permission to grant permissions is equivalent to holding all of them

column5: Global Administrator, by assigning the directory role to itself
column6: directory roles are separate from Azure RBAC; subscription-level controls do not constrain this

column5: group membership, which frequently gates access granted elsewhere
column6: adding a principal to a group inherits whatever that group was given

column5: activation into privileged roles managed through PIM
column6: relevant only where PIM governs the roles that matter

column5: every credential stored in the vault, each of which is a fresh input for a second run
column6: queued deliberately rather than followed; auto-recursion turns one authorized test into an unbounded one

column5: full control of every service in the account, and SAS tokens minted from the key
column6: an account key is unscoped and unexpiring, so it is closer to a permanent backdoor than a credential
